facts.title: The Last Stable Myth
facts.text: For two centuries bismuth-209 was considered the heaviest stable isotope in nature. In 2003 French physicists at the Institut d'Astrophysique Spatiale in Orsay measured it actually undergoing alpha decay with a half-life of about 20 billion billion years (2.01 x 10^19 years). That is more than a billion times the current age of the universe, so a chunk of bismuth is, for any practical purpose, eternal.

facts.title: A White Metal With a Misleading Name
facts.text: The name likely comes from the German Weisse Masse or Wismut, meaning white mass, later Latinized to bisemutum. Although early miners often confused it with lead and tin, Claude Geoffroy the Younger demonstrated in 1753 that bismuth is a distinct element. It remains one of the few elements known since antiquity yet only formally identified in the modern chemical era.

facts.title: It Expands When It Freezes
facts.text: Like water, gallium, and antimony, bismuth is one of the rare substances that expands as it solidifies, growing about 3.3 percent in volume. This makes solid bismuth less dense than its own liquid, so a chunk will float on the molten metal. The property historically made it valuable in type-metal alloys, because the expansion forced the metal sharply into every detail of a printing mould.

facts.title: The Most Diamagnetic Metal
facts.text: Bismuth is the most strongly diamagnetic of all metals, meaning it is repelled by magnetic fields rather than attracted. A small bismuth slab can help levitate a tiny magnet by passively pushing back against it. This same electronic structure also gives bismuth an unusually large Hall effect and very low thermal conductivity for a metal.

facts.title: Rainbow Crystals From the Lab
facts.text: When molten bismuth cools slowly it forms striking hopper crystals: stair-stepped, geometric structures with a brilliant oil-slick iridescence. The colors are not the metal itself but a thin oxide layer that forms on the surface and creates thin-film interference, splitting white light into pinks, blues, golds, and purples. These crystals are a favorite of chemistry demonstrations and mineral collectors precisely because they are easy to grow at home.

facts.title: The Pink Stuff in Your Medicine Cabinet
facts.text: Bismuth subsalicylate is the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol and similar stomach remedies. It coats the digestive lining, has a mild antibacterial action, and is even used as part of combination therapy against Helicobacter pylori, the bacterium behind many stomach ulcers. Bismuth compounds have soothed upset stomachs since the 18th century, making this heavy metal a surprisingly gentle medicine.

facts.title: A Green Replacement for Lead
facts.text: Because bismuth sits just next to lead on the periodic table but is far less toxic, industry increasingly uses it as a non-toxic substitute. It appears in lead-free solders, free-machining brasses, fishing sinkers, and even some shotgun pellets. This shift matters for environmental and worker safety, letting manufacturers keep useful density and low melting points without lead's well-known health hazards.

facts.title: Metal That Melts in Hot Water
facts.text: Alloyed with lead, tin, cadmium, or indium, bismuth forms fusible alloys with astonishingly low melting points. Field's metal melts at about 62 degrees Celsius and Wood's metal at around 70 degrees, both below the boiling point of water. These alloys are used in fire-sprinkler triggers and electrical fuses, where a small temperature rise melts the metal and sets off a safety response.

facts.title: Forged in Dying Stars
facts.text: Bismuth is created in the cosmos mainly through the slow neutron-capture process, the s-process, inside aging red giant stars. Lighter nuclei capture neutrons one at a time over thousands of years, climbing the chart of isotopes until they reach bismuth. Because the next steps lead to unstable, rapidly decaying elements, bismuth marks a natural endpoint of this stellar nucleosynthesis pathway.

facts.title: Rare and Quietly Useful
facts.text: Bismuth makes up only about 8.5 parts per billion of Earth's crust, making it roughly as scarce as silver. It is mostly recovered as a byproduct of refining lead, copper, and tin ores rather than mined on its own. Despite its rarity, it finds work in cosmetics as pearlescent bismuth oxychloride, in pigments, and as a catalyst, proving that even an uncommon element can be remarkably versatile.
